title: Tilenus: Rome slanders us as Pelagians; Adam's will was naturally upright but moved to act by grace, like a vine needing sun and rain
source_text: XXXIX. Quibus similia apud Tilenum legere est. Criminose, inquit, & calumniose Pelagianorum sententiam nobis affingunt Pontificii, quasi nulla supernaturalia dona in primo homine fuisse contendamus, cum Theologicas virtutes ipsi tribuamus διαρρήδην. De justitia Originali thesi trigesima octava. Paulo ante vero distinctius explicans qua in re consisteret gratia Adamo collata, Ut a natura, inquit, id habebat voluntas Adami, ut posset juste & sancte operari, sic ut reapse operaretur, Deumque super omnia amaret, efficaciter movebatur a gratia. At quemadmodum vitis non propterea caret vi naturali ad proferendum vinum, quod externis illi opus est auxiliis, puta sole, pluvia & cultura, ut actu proferat, sic & in Adamo non ideo naturalis non fuit voluntatis rectitudo, & affectuum εὐταξία, licet in actu secundo gratiae moventis auxilio exercitaretur & adjuvaretur.
pass_a_gloss: Things similar to which may be read in Tilenus. Criminally, he says, and calumniously the Papists fasten on us the opinion of the Pelagians, as if we contended that there were no supernatural gifts in the first man, when we attribute the Theological virtues to him expressly. On Original justice thesis thirty-eight. But a little before, explaining more distinctly in what the grace conferred on Adam consisted, As Adam's will had this from nature, he says, that it could work justly and holily, so that it should actually work, and love God above all, it was efficaciously moved by grace. But as a vine does not on that account lack natural force for producing wine, that it needs external aids, for instance sun, rain and cultivation, in order to produce in act, so also in Adam the rectitude of the will, and eutaxia of the affections, was not on that account not natural, although in second act it was exercised and helped by the aid of moving grace.
pass_b_english: Similar things can be read in Tilenus: "The papists wickedly and slanderously pin the Pelagians' view on us, as though we held there were no supernatural gifts in the first man, when we expressly ascribe the theological virtues to him." (On Original Righteousness, thesis 38.)

A little earlier, explaining more precisely what the grace given to Adam consisted in, he says: "Adam's will had from nature the power to act righteously and holily; that it actually did so, and loved God above all things, came from its being moved effectively by grace.

"But a vine is not without a natural power to bear wine just because it needs outside help, such as sun, rain and tending, to bear it in fact. In the same way the uprightness of Adam's will and the good order (eutaxia) of his affections were still natural, even though in their actual exercise they were set to work and helped by moving grace."

choices.why: Le Blanc's period term for adherents of the papacy, used by Tilenus in polemic; kept as historical usage.
